name: Retinalamin
lead: Retinalamin is a polypeptide extract prepared from the retinas of cattle or pigs. It was developed in Russia within the group of gerontologist Vladimir Khavinson and belongs to the family of animal-tissue-derived peptide preparations that this group calls cytomedins or peptide bioregulators [4]. It is used clinically in Russia and neighbouring countries, mainly by injection, for retinal conditions such as glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy [1][3][6].

Published human research consists largely of Russian-language studies in the journal Vestnik oftalmologii, in which Retinalamin was given alongside standard care to people with glaucoma whose eye pressure was already controlled. These reports describe improvements in some structural and functional measures compared with control groups [1][3]. Laboratory studies describe effects on retinal and pigment epithelial cell proliferation in culture [2].

Retinalamin is not an appearance product. It appears in longevity-peptide discussions because it is listed together with other Khavinson preparations such as Epithalamin and Prostatilen [4]. Much of the supporting literature comes from the developer's own research network, and the review summarising it was written by the same group [4].

paras: Retinalamin is described as a polypeptide preparation isolated from retinal tissue [2]. It is grouped by its developers among peptide bioregulators, a class they propose as geroprotectors, meaning substances intended to slow age-related decline [4]. Its tissue-specific retinal origin is said to give it a targeted effect on the retina, an idea the group has tested in cell culture, including work on retinal ganglion cells [9].

Wikipedia describes Vladimir Khavinson (27 November 1946 to 6 January 2024) as a Russian gerontologist who directed the Saint Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology and headed a gerontology chair at North-Western State Medical University.[12] The article says he worked on peptide bioregulators from 1973 to 2013, extracting peptides from animal organs and synthesising others, and that six peptide preparations, among them Thymalin, Epithalamin and Cortexin, were approved for medical use in the USSR and Russia, mainly in military medicine.[12] It describes Retinalamin as a retinal preparation that partially restores retinal function after laser lesions and in degenerative disease.[12]

The same Wikipedia entry carries maintenance notices that its field-of-work section contains promotional content and that its statements about the peptides lacking adverse effects rest on Khavinson's own studies without independent verification.[12] Researchers outside the developer's network have not published comparable trials in the sources surveyed here.

Most clinical reports come from Russian ophthalmology. A randomised study of 180 patients (355 eyes) with open-angle glaucoma and normalised intraocular pressure compared intramuscular Retinalamin courses, repeated after six months, with a control group over 12 months, assessing visual function and retinal structure [1]. A second randomised study of 147 patients (249 eyes) with stage I-II primary open-angle glaucoma examined whether courses repeated every six months affected disease progression on structural and functional tests [3]. Further reports covered neuroprotective therapy results in glaucoma [10], an optical coherence tomography angiography pilot study [7] and functional monitoring in diabetic retinopathy [6].

A review by Khavinson's group summarising its long-term clinical work on several bioregulators, Retinalamin among them, reports benefits in prevention and treatment across age groups [4]. The studies are published in regional journals, and independent replication in Western trials is not documented in the available literature.

In the 180-patient randomized study, visual acuity and intraocular pressure did not change significantly in either group over 12 months, but the visual field mean deviation index in the Retinalamin group improved from about -5.5 to -4.8 dB while it worsened in controls from about -3.5 to -4.6 dB; the pattern standard deviation index moved in opposite directions in the two groups as well.[1] In the 147-patient study with 24 months of follow-up, visual acuity and refraction did not change in either group, intraocular pressure rose in the control group, and the authors compared structural and perimetry measures between groups across the period.[3]

A third randomized study of 146 patients with stage I to III glaucoma, allocated 2:1, added one 10-injection intramuscular course to standard neuroprotective therapy and reported wider visual fields, better uncorrected visual acuity and contrast sensitivity, and shorter photostress recovery over three months, with no adverse events during the course.[10] An earlier gerontology report said Retinalamin in elderly patients with involutional eye disease was associated with better vision function and quality of life.[11]

In vitro, Retinalamin and the synthetic peptide Epithalon were reported to stimulate proliferation of retinal and pigment epithelial cells in a tissue-specific way at certain concentrations [2]. A further paper examined inductive activity of retinal peptides [5], and another discussed delivery and efficacy of peptide bioregulators [8].

card.summary: Animal-derived retinal peptide extract from Russia, studied in glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy; no appearance use is documented.
card.note: Evidence is mostly Russian-language studies from the developer's research network; not an appearance product.

quick.overview:
Retinalamin is a peptide extract made from animal retinas, developed in Russia by Vladimir Khavinson's group. It is used there by injection for eye conditions such as glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy.

It shows up in longevity-peptide lists next to other Khavinson preparations. No studies examine it for appearance.
quick.mechanism: Its developers describe it as a tissue-specific peptide complex that supports retinal cells. Cell-culture work reports stimulation of retinal and pigment epithelial cell proliferation.
quick.risks: Published safety data come mainly from Russian studies by the developer's network. It is not approved as a drug in most Western countries, and independent Western trials are not documented.
